title: Here the World in Stereo: Learning Dynamic Spatial Correspondence for Immersive Joint Video-Audio Generation

details.title: Here the World in Stereo: Learning Dynamic Spatial Correspondence for Immersive Joint Video-Audio Generation
details.abstract: Recent joint video-audio generation models have achieved strong semantic correspondence and temporal synchronization. However, applications such as AR/VR and interactive gaming further require stereo audio to provide an immersive sense, which remains largely overlooked. Effective stereo audio requires the perceived sound location to evolve consistently with the motion of its corresponding visual source. We refer to this property as Dynamic Spatial Correspondence and propose StereoBind, a framework that binds visual source motion to stereo sound generation. StereoBind uses motion tracks to coordinate visual motion and stereo audio through three complementary mechanisms. Visual Motion Binding establishes source-aware audiovisual correspondence, the Spatial Track Encoder captures absolute source positions, and Residual Track RoPE models relative motion. For supervision and evaluation, we construct StereoWorld-29K, a large-scale stereo audio-video dataset with paired motion tracks, and StereoWorldBench for measuring audiovisual spatial consistency. Experiments show that StereoBind substantially improves spatial alignment in stereo audio generation over existing models while preserving overall audiovisual quality.

title: VisionWeave: Weaving Elastic Visual Representations as a Native Capability of MLLMs

details.title: VisionWeave: Weaving Elastic Visual Representations as a Native Capability of MLLMs
details.abstract: We're excited to share our latest work, VisionWeave! As multimodal models move toward long-horizon interaction with both digital and real-world environments, visual token efficiency has become a critical bottleneck for practical deployment. We argue that the key is to let models natively operate over elastic visual representations — a capability we call VisionWeave. Over the past year, sparse attention has evolved from a post-training trick into a native model capability. We believe visual token efficiency holds the same promise. Building on prior ideas from this line of research, VisionWeave pushes efficiency from a task-specific trick toward a robust, model-native paradigm. Validated on the frontier Qwen3.8-27B: The model adaptively weaves visual representations of mixed granularities conditioned on the input content, enabling adaptive, efficient understanding Extensively evaluated across 8 domain benchmarks × multiple resolution tiers × multiple video frame rates Saves 43.0% of visual tokens on average while retaining 98.9% of native performance Under SGLang deployment: 2.30× throughput and 54.4% lower TTFT Efficiency, robustness, and real-world deployability — all in one native capability. We believe weaving elastic visual representations can become a built-in ability of future models, paving the way for efficient, long-horizon interaction between multimodal foundation models and their visual environments. arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07987

title: Inducing Process Supervision from Outcome-Only Reinforcement Learning

details.title: Inducing Process Supervision from Outcome-Only Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: Can strong process reward models emerge from outcome-only reinforcement learning? We introduce TIPS (Thinking-Induced Process Supervision), a simple framework that trains generative PRMs using only outcome-level correctness rewards, without human step annotations, Monte Carlo rollouts, or explicit process supervision. By rewarding accurate outcome judgments, TIPS implicitly encourages models to verify intermediate reasoning steps. With just 3.2K outcome-labeled trajectories, TIPS-Qwen3-4B-Thinking achieves 85.2 F1 on ProcessBench, outperforming all evaluated trained PRMs and strong proprietary LLM judges, including GPT-5.4-Instruct and Claude-4.7-Opus. Our results suggest that process supervision can emerge from outcome-only RL, offering a scalable and cost-effective path toward stronger reasoning verification. Code: https://github.com/RUCBM/TIPS

title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers

details.title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers
details.abstract: TL;DR: Can a plain Transformer generate high-quality images directly in pixel space, with no VAE and no specialized pixel decoder? We show that it can, provided its internal representation is both properly formed and actively exploited . 🔍 Two insights Better representations ≠ better generation. REPA-style alignment improves semantics at the aligned layer, but the gain fades in later layers and does not improve final FID. Pixel decoders mostly shift work around. PixelDiT, DiP, and DeCo change how semantic and spatial modeling is split between encoder and decoder, but they do not yield representations better suited to generation. 💡 Representation Guidance (RG) A low-dimensional bottleneck packs generation-relevant information into a compact implicit latent. The decoder's velocity with vs. without the representation gives an offset, which we use to modify the flow-matching target : v_RG = v + (s-1)·sg(Δv_rep) . This forces the decoder to depend on the representation, and in turn shapes the encoder toward what synthesis needs. This works like self-distillation in SSL: the representation is bootstrapped from the model's own predictions. 📈 Results ImageNet 256: FID 1.55 (RG-XL/16, 725M). RG-L/16 with only 459M params beats much larger pixel DiTs, including the 2B JiT-G. 4× faster convergence : RG-B reaches JiT-B's 600-epoch FID in 150 epochs. ImageNet 512: FID 1.74 . Text-to-image: GenEval 0.89 / DPG-Bench 87.1 . 🌐 Project: https://pan-zihao.github.io/Representation-Guidance/ 💻 Code: https://github.com/Pan-Zihao/Representation-Guidance

title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control

details.title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
details.abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.

title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents

details.title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents
details.abstract: Hi everyone👋 Static coding benchmarks don't last long. Their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents saturate them. In SWE-Duel, we try a different approach: coding agents create tasks for each other at evaluation time, so there's nothing to leak in advance, and the difficulty grows with the agents themselves. How it works: two agents take turns as Red and Blue on a real repository. Red adds a new feature, then hides a subtle bug in it, with sealed tests that trigger the bug. The task only counts if a fresh session of the same agent can fix the bug blind, so there are no unsolvable tasks. Blue reviews the PR without being told there's a bug. It wins only if its revision passes the feature tests, the existing tests, and the hidden bug tests. Then they swap roles. We ran 1,500 turns with 11 model-harness pairs on 15 repos in 5 languages. A few findings: GPT-5.5 + Codex CLI ranks 1st as the strongest solver, fixing 98.3% of the bugs it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 + mini-swe-agent ranks 2nd as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Within one model family, tasks written by the newest version beat a fixed reference solver far more often than those from older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%). This suggests task difficulty scales with the agents' own ability. Happy to answer any questions!

title: GraphDecisionBench: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks

details.title: GraphDecisionBench: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks
details.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for graph understanding and decision-making, while System One models such as Jev select directly from supplied options. However, the capabilities of System One models on graph-related tasks remain unclear. We introduce GraphDecide, a model-independent benchmark that combines structural task profiles, matched graph-text input contrasts and heuristic-proposal controls to diagnose graph decision performance. We evaluate Jev and related choice-based models alongside language-model baselines, covering fourteen model-interface configurations. Jev's results illustrate the benchmark's central distinctions: accurate adjacency recognition does not guarantee broader structural correctness, joint graph-text input does not consistently improve prediction, and feasible construction does not establish high solution quality. Its task contracts, candidate interfaces and scoring rules support comparison across native selectors and language-model adapters. Code and aggregate results are available at https://github.com/VictorYXL/GraphDecisionBench .

title: Rethinking Relative Policy Differences Transfer of On-Policy Distillation

details.title: Rethinking Relative Policy Differences Transfer of On-Policy Distillation
details.abstract: Can on-policy distillation transfer an improvement without requiring a stronger teacher? In Rethinking Relative Policy Differences Transfer of On-Policy Distillation, we study how the log-probability difference between a proxy expert and a proxy reference can guide a target model on its own rollouts. Our any-to-any OPD formulation treats this difference as an implicit reward and recovers conventional OPD as a special case. We find that differences created by RL or SFT transfer more reliably than those arising from model scale alone. The expert supplies the capability, the reference isolates the part to transfer, and the target must be able to learn and generalize the resulting update. These findings offer practical guidance for choosing source pairs and targets—including cases where changing the reference turns a failed transfer into a successful one. Code: https://github.com/KnowledgeXLab/A2-OPD

title: From Given to Gathered Evidence: Agentic Learning for Longitudinal Medical Reasoning

details.title: From Given to Gathered Evidence: Agentic Learning for Longitudinal Medical Reasoning
details.abstract: CASE: From Given to Gathered Evidence Clinical reasoning is not merely about interpreting evidence, but also about knowing what evidence to seek. Existing medical AI benchmarks primarily evaluate reasoning over preselected information, overlooking the ability to autonomously gather, compare, and synthesize evidence across clinical records and longitudinal imaging. We introduce CASE (Clinical Agents for Seeking Evidence) , shifting medical AI from passive question answering to active, evidence-grounded clinical investigation . Key Contributions Longitudinal Multimodal Benchmark. A UK Biobank-based benchmark comprising 50,401 clinical questions from 4,739 participants , integrating clinical records and multi-sequence MRI across baseline and follow-up visits. Autonomous Evidence-Seeking Agents. A role-conditioned, multi-tool framework enabling compact vision-language models to autonomously select visits, modalities, anatomical structures, image slices, and specialist tools for evidence collection and cross-visit reasoning. Beyond Teacher Imitation. An agentic post-training framework integrating Agentic RL, On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), and RLAIF to improve evidence-to-conclusion reasoning while preserving autonomous tool-use decisions.

title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution

details.title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution
details.abstract: We introduce Video-RSI , a framework for recursive self-improvement of video understanding agents through harness evolution. Instead of updating model weights, Video-RSI enables the agent to revisit the original training videos used for evolution, gather additional visual, transcript, and OCR evidence, and test competing explanations for its failures. Evidence-supported diagnoses are then translated into reusable changes to the agent’s prompts, tools, memory, and execution logic. Video-RSI uses a cost-aware selection process to retain revisions based on both answer accuracy and visual processing cost. Across the evaluated video understanding benchmarks, the evolved harness improves accuracy while processing fewer frames, yielding competitive accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. We release the inference and evaluation code, the initial and final harnesses, and the implementation of the harness-evolution workflow. We welcome feedback and discussion from the community.

title: Judging in Latent Space: Efficient Generative Reward Modeling via Semantics-Preserving Compression

details.title: Judging in Latent Space: Efficient Generative Reward Modeling via Semantics-Preserving Compression
details.abstract: The interesting idea here is that a reward model doesn’t need to spell out every evaluation step to make a good judgment. LatentGRM compresses rubric-based reasoning into continuous latent states, keeping judgment accuracy competitive while cutting inference time by roughly 6–7× in the reported 8B experiments at vote@5. The rubric interventions are especially interesting: changing evaluation criteria changes the resulting preferences, suggesting that the latent trajectories retain criterion-specific information. There’s also an offline interpreter that recovers evaluation text from teacher-derived trajectories. It’s a promising way to make reasoning-heavy judges cheaper, with some visibility into what survives compression.

title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals

details.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
details.abstract: Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR) , an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of 1.58× over the standard residual baseline, compared with 1.35× for AttnRes and 1.30× for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.

title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning

details.title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
details.abstract: With SpatialASM, we explore whether LVLMs can go beyond passively observing the given images and instead actively reason by planning task-relevant viewpoints and mentally imagining what should be visible from them. We introduce Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM) and build a scalable training framework around it. SpatialASM uses an allocentric novel-view generator as training-time scaffolding to synthesize explicit plan-imagine-reason trajectories and automatically verifiable perspective-taking tasks. In this way, models learn both when to seek missing spatial evidence and how to reconstruct it internally without requiring additional views or a renderer at inference time. This is our attempt to bring a more human-like form of active spatial exploration into LVLMs and alleviate the scarcity of high-quality spatial reasoning supervision. Across four LVLM backbones and seven spatial benchmarks, SpatialASM improves spatial reasoning performance while preserving general visual capabilities. We’d love to hear your thoughts and feedback!

title: Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation: Formulation, Benchmark, and Method

details.title: Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation: Formulation, Benchmark, and Method
details.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) has largely focused on a single agent following a single instruction, yet many real-world applications require teams of robots to tackle tasks beyond the capabilities of any individual agent. We present Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation, the first systematic formalization of multi-agent VLN as a constrained coordination problem: each mission consists of subtasks carrying dependency and resource constraints (presence locks and holding chains). MAVLN is a benchmark built with a verified four-stage crafting pipeline. It contains 11,724 episodes across 145 HM3D scenes, with teams of up to four agents under three instruction regimes, and comes with constraint-aware metrics. TRISS is a coordination-ready navigation system. It couples an LLM-based subtask scheduler, a shared topological memory that turns each agent's exploration into team knowledge, and a conflict-aware execution mechanism that realizes simultaneous intentions as collision-free routes. Extensive experiments establish TRISS as a comprehensive baseline and reveal substantial room for improvement across scheduling, navigation, and execution.

title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training

details.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
details.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.

title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces

details.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
details.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce Panini-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate Panini-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven baseline implementations using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. Panini-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks, with strong gains on harder questions. On BrowseComp-Plus, Panini-DR achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best baseline by 16.0 percentage points, at higher inference cost. Its advantage is strongest on harder investigations, correctly answering 26 of 50 hard questions—nearly twice as many as the next-best baseline. Our ablation studies further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does verification combined with evidence checks. To assess whether correct answers are supported by the research performed, we also analyze the evidence retained by each system. Panini-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how systems compare and further strengthens Panini-DR's advantage over existing approaches.

title: PhyProbe: Rethinking Physical Consistency Evaluation in Generated Videos

details.title: PhyProbe: Rethinking Physical Consistency Evaluation in Generated Videos

title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning

details.title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning

title: Scoring Higher, Answering Worse: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL via Protocol-Level Rubrics

details.title: Scoring Higher, Answering Worse: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL via Protocol-Level Rubrics
details.abstract: Can an AI get a better score by giving a worse answer? Surprisingly, yes. Imagine asking whether to call 911—and getting 2,000+ characters of explanation before the model tells you to call. The answer checks plenty of boxes, but misses what matters: getting the urgent advice to you immediately. We found that rubric-based RL can encourage this behavior. When checklist scores simply add up, models can earn points for extra details that compensate for a critical mistake. ProRubric changes how those points are earned. Related requirements must pass together, and a critical failure wipes out the group’s credit. On Qwen3-4B, this improves appropriateness by 10.8 points over standard Rubric-RL without sacrificing rubric coverage. The takeaway: better checklists are only half the story—how we score them matters too.

Building on this insight, we propose Ares, an adaptive-rank optimizer that dynamically aligns optimization with the evolving gradient structure. We hope this work inspires a new perspective on optimizer design for LLM reinforcement learning!

title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence

details.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence
details.abstract: Hi HF community! I'm Yang Xiao , the first author of Vela. As LLMs are deployed across more real-world scenarios, they must be able to learn from long-term context, understand users' evolving preferences and intent, and make decisions grounded in behavioral evidence. These capabilities provide a foundation for organizations deploying LLMs in high-value real-world scenarios, including complex decision-making, long-term planning and autonomous agent execution. Vela explores anonymized user behavior as supervision to develop these capabilities and strengthen broader LLM intelligence . Vela converts behavior histories from 100K users into tasks across 91 templates. Filtering and trajectory selection retain approximately 75K training examples. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B improves performance on all ten evaluated benchmarks. Compared with the base model, Vela gains 11.5 points on VelaBench , with average gains of 6.2 points across four independent user-related benchmarks and 4.0 points across five general benchmarks . Behavior records were anonymized before task construction. Their use was platform-authorized and underwent privacy and ethics review. Happy to discuss the method, evaluation and applications!

title: AutoEnvScaling: Automating the Data Flywheel with Terminal Agents

details.title: AutoEnvScaling: Automating the Data Flywheel with Terminal Agents
details.abstract: Recursive self-improvement needs agents that can build their own training environments. But researchers still sit in the loop, limiting it to scale. We introduce AutoEnvScaling, which turns env design into a terminal task: a proposer agent builds complete Harbor tasks, each with a Docker image, instruction, solution, and tests. It runs and debugs them just like human researchers before submission. This enables self-play RL for terminal agents: a single model improves as both environment builder and solver, without humans writing each new task and its tests.

title: CURIO: Curiosity-Driven Test-Time Learning for Open-Ended Discovery

details.title: CURIO: Curiosity-Driven Test-Time Learning for Open-Ended Discovery
details.abstract: CURIO: Curiosity-Driven Test-Time Learning for Open-Ended Discovery Test-time RL lets an LLM actually learn from its own attempts on a discovery problem, but reward-only updates tend to collapse onto early high-reward trajectories and kill off directions that look bad now but could pay off later. CURIO adds a curiosity signal to test-time RL : 🧠 Intrinsic Curiosity World Model (ICWM): learns transitions in the policy’s own hidden-state space and gives prediction-error bonuses to sampled tokens outside the policy’s top-k, rewarding genuinely novel reasoning instead of random noise. ⚖️ Stable integration: epoch-wise normalization and an annealed curiosity weight keep the bonus as a complement to task reward, so it doesn’t override it. Results (Qwen3-8B to 235B) : 📐 Beats a matched task-only RL baseline on 5 of 6 math discovery objectives, and matches the best reported result on Circle Packing 🧬 Improves single-cell denoising Score and MSE on both held-out corpora at every scale tested 📈 Up to +18.3% on Hadamard and +10.8% on denoising Score 🌱 Generated programs are measurably more structurally diverse

title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer

details.title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer
details.abstract: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present ShellElastic, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce $\mu$-Elastic, an extension of maximal update parameterization ($\mu$P) to ShellElastic and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously ($\mu$-Internal), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets ($\mu$-Transfer). A single ShellElastic run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.

title: Any Time, Any Space: A World-State-Centric Framework for Agentic Video Generation

details.title: Any Time, Any Space: A World-State-Centric Framework for Agentic Video Generation
details.abstract: Excited to share ATAS — Any Time, Any Space ! Video models can produce impressive individual shots, but keeping a whole story consistent is harder: a room should keep its layout when revisited, and different cameras should capture the same event at the same point in time. We introduce ATAS , a world-state-centric framework that gives video agents a shared spatial and temporal reference. 🧠 Two complementary memories : scene memory stores registered static geometry, while event memory stores time-indexed dynamic observations. Each new shot retrieves the evidence it needs. 🎥 Different cameras, one event : agents can revisit earlier locations or replay past events from new viewpoints, querying the same evolving world state. 📊 Evaluated across four video generators : ATAS improves the reported cross-shot consistency measures, with further evaluations covering spatial revisits, event recapture, and human preferences. Any Time, Any Space. Every shot has a history. 🌐 Project page & interactive demo 💻 Code 🎬 Promo video Try the demo to explore the point clouds, camera poses, and linked videos!

title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation

details.title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation
details.abstract: We introduce LatentLoop, which improves looped MoE models under matched budgets by compressing the first loop visit, preserving full resolution in the second, and reallocating the saved compute to increase model width.

title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory

details.title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
details.abstract: How can multimodal agents remember what they perceive, keep that memory useful as the world changes, and learn to manage it better over time? We are sharing our survey, “Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory.” We organize this growing field around two complementary axes: 🔹 Formation and Representation: How is multimodal information stored—as modality-specific representations, text and structured records, latent or parametric memory, or hybrid representations that preserve links to the original evidence? 🔹 Memory Management: How does memory adapt over time? We distinguish static memory , dynamic memory updated through a stable policy, and self-evolving memory whose management policy improves through experience. A central distinction is that updating memory content and improving the policy that manages memory are different capabilities . Our framework helps clarify this difference and connects memory design to evidence preservation, temporal consistency, and reliable reasoning across long-horizon tasks. The survey also covers memory infrastructure, evaluation benchmarks, applications, and open challenges. We hope it serves as a useful guide for researchers and practitioners building multimodal agents. We welcome feedback, discussion, and suggestions for relevant work!

title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation

details.title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
details.abstract: Developed jointly by JD.com’s OxygenVLM team and Nanjing University, RoadMOPD mitigates learning conflicts among teachers with substantially different response styles and domain expertise, helping a student integrate multiple experts’ capabilities while reducing degradation in individual domains. It brings routed and auxiliary teachers together to evaluate the same student-generated response, using teacher agreement to strengthen jointly supported token-level corrections and attenuate conflicting signals. Preventive gradient projection then suppresses conflicting update components while adaptively preserving the target domain’s learning signal. With Qwen3-4B, RoadMOPD improves both domains over Vanilla MOPD in the high-conflict Math–Medical and Code–Medical settings, boosting average medical accuracy by up to 8.78 percentage points. Benefits also extend to the more compatible Math–Code combination, with improvements across all three domains under joint Math–Code–Medical training. The code is currently undergoing internal company approval for open-source release and is expected to be released within the next 1–2 months.

title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents

details.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
details.abstract: Your LLM agent has to think out loud, token by token, before it can search, run code, or act in the world. We humans don’t. We ponder in silence and speak when it matters. Human language was never meant to be the limit of machine thought. Introducing 🌗 Hybrid Reasoning Agents Think in latent space, act through text Two modes, one unified multi-turn flow No black box, fully readable latent thoughts Any LLM can become a HybridAgent

title: APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation

details.title: APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation
details.abstract: Better models. Smarter training data. Different image models struggle with different things. A fixed training set cannot keep up with every model’s evolving strengths and weaknesses. APT makes post-training adaptive. Three agents work together to evaluate the current model, diagnose its failure modes, and generate the training prompts it needs next. After each update, the loop starts again. APT (Agentic Post-Training) turns post-training into a fully automated, evaluation-driven adaptive loop. Given a user-specified evaluation scope, the Evaluation Set Generation Agent constructs a diverse evaluation set consisting of prompt–evaluation rubric pairs; the Diagnosis Agent evaluates the current model on these pairs to identify its strengths and failure modes; and the RL Data Generation Agent adaptively samples next-round training prompts, prioritizing underperforming capabilities. The updated model is then re-evaluated in the next round, allowing the training distribution to continuously adapt to the model's evolving capability profile. This design eliminates the need for manually curated post-training data and makes APT model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully automated.

title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation

details.title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation
details.abstract: 🤖 CriticOPD: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation 🔍 Key finding: Teachers can recognize student mistakes yet still follow them when continuing a flawed solution, making OPD supervision unreliable. ✍️ Our approach: The teacher uses the reference answer to critique incorrect student rollouts, and the student rewrites the continuation with this feedback. The teacher scores the rewritten suffix with the feedback in context, while the student learns from that suffix without seeing the feedback. 📈 Results: Across six math reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves average accuracy over OPD by 4.57 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B and 4.06 on Qwen3-0.6B , with the largest gains on competition problems. 🌐 Project page · 💻 Code

title: HumanoidToolBench: Benchmarking Humanoid Tool Use from Selection to Mobile Execution

details.title: HumanoidToolBench: Benchmarking Humanoid Tool Use from Selection to Mobile Execution
details.abstract: Can humanoids choose the right tool and then actually use it? We introduce HumanoidToolBench, an 18-task benchmark evaluating humanoid tool selection and execution across three scenarios, three execution levels, and two tool-set modes. We also introduce ToolBook, a dataset of 3.1k demonstrations collected in simulation and on a real Unitree G1. Evaluating seven policies in simulation and three on the real robot reveals a substantial gap between selecting a suitable tool and successfully completing the task. Additional GR00T N1.7 probes examine generalization to unseen tools and behavior under unrelated instructions. Explore the benchmark and demonstrations on our project page. We welcome feedback from the humanoid learning and tool-use communities!

title: RAR: Rate-Adaptive Rollout for Time-Consistent Interactive World Models

details.title: RAR: Rate-Adaptive Rollout for Time-Consistent Interactive World Models
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We’re sharing RAR (Rate-Adaptive Rollout), a framework for controllable generation rates in interactive world models. Most world models run at a fixed temporal rate, so differences in hardware throughput can unintentionally speed up or slow down the generated world. RAR combines physical-time-aligned Stride-RoPE with synchronized multi-stride training, enabling one model to generate at multiple rates—including unseen intermediate rates—and switch rates mid-rollout without resetting the KV cache. This makes it possible to match the rollout rate to runtime throughput while keeping the world’s physical-time progression consistent. Happy to discuss and hear your feedback!

title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning

details.title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: We present a large-scale, systematic evaluation of self-distillation methods in agentic reinforcement learning, revealing that existing methods struggle to consistently outperform GRPO despite increased computational costs. We hope our work provides the community with a fair and reliable benchmark, encouraging future research toward more robust, stable, and cost-effective agent training.

title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning

details.title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: ScreenRef and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning (D2RL) are the core contributions of GroundGUI. ScreenRef is a high-quality GUI grounding dataset spanning desktop, web, and mobile environments. It pairs diverse screenshots with referring expressions and localization annotations, covering text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal. Building on ScreenRef, we train GroundGUI-8B from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with supervised fine-tuning and D2RL, improving precise localization in complex interfaces.

title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents

details.title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
details.abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.

title: Physical Time as a Missing Dimension of Robot Policy Memory Dynamics

details.title: Physical Time as a Missing Dimension of Robot Policy Memory Dynamics
details.abstract: Robot policies act in physical time, but their memories are often organized around observation steps. What happens when these two clocks disagree? The same observation history can require different actions depending on how much time has elapsed. A robot making tea may see an unchanged scene, yet need to switch from waiting to lifting. The same observed displacement can imply different velocities, changing how a robot should intercept an object after it disappears from view. Remembering what happened is only part of the challenge; a policy must also determine what that history means now. We introduce Temporal Flow Policy (TFP), which makes physical time part of policy memory dynamics. Current observations and retained history shape each memory transition, while measured elapsed time determines how far the state advances. The resulting memory guides diffusion and flow-matching policies through their native imitation objectives. Through controlled comparisons, interventions on the supplied clock, and real-robot experiments, we investigate how retained history and physical time jointly shape behavior. TFP explores a broader design principle for robot learning: the internal state used for action should reflect both the history of observations and the physical time over which that history unfolds.

title: Long-Horizon RL Needs Muon

details.title: Long-Horizon RL Needs Muon
details.abstract: Long-horizon agents must coordinate reasoning, tool use, and environment feedback over extended interactions. Learning from sparse outcome rewards requires weighting trajectories of different lengths and updating the policy while rollouts are still being collected. We examine a single-rollout asynchronous recipe combining Muon , token-averaged loss, truncated importance sampling, and auxiliary length and tool-error penalties. Single-rollout sampling allows asynchronous learning without waiting for multiple trajectories for the same issue. We study optimizer choices and recipe components for repository-level issue resolution across two model families. The evaluated training runs show higher training success with the full recipe than with the baselines.

title: Acting Through Registers

details.title: Acting Through Registers
details.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.

title: Exploring the Limits of Combinatorial Generalization in Embodied Manipulation

details.title: Exploring the Limits of Combinatorial Generalization in Embodied Manipulation
details.abstract: In embodied manipulation, Vision Language Action (VLA) models can execute atomic skills, but long-horizon manipulation requires recombining these skills without demonstrations for every skill combination. The full instruction route treats skill chaining as long-horizon imitation. In a controlled study, full instruction training on limited skill combination sequences reaches 40.0% ordered success on covered combinations but only 7.7% on recombination, suggesting memorization of sequence templates rather than robust skill recombination. We introduce Hierarchical Subtask Execution (HSE), a diagnostic framework that exposes skill recombination through a shared modular interface over the planner, trigger, and policy, decomposing long-horizon failures into separable modes. We introduce RoboCombine, a benchmark for skill recombination without combined skill training trajectories, with metrics for ordered success and transition conversion across subtask boundaries. RoboCombine reveals that atomic competence alone does not ensure ordered execution. Failures concentrate at transitions where downstream subtasks launch from handoff states from preceding subtasks rather than canonical atomic starts. We identify this mismatch as the start state gap. To address it, we introduce Pose Robust Task Initialization (PRTI), a lightweight atomic task post-training strategy that broadens start state coverage beyond canonical starts. Under oracle timed HSE on RoboCombine, PRTI reaches 18.16% ordered success, compared with 4.21% under random perturbation and 9.47% under a robot-reset oracle, without combined skill training trajectories. These results show that combinatorial generalization requires handoff robust atomic skills that convert first stage progress into reliable downstream execution, not merely decomposition into known subtasks.

title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing

details.title: Diff Diffusion: Predicting Edit Paths with Diffusion Models for Efficient Code Editing
details.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are appealing for code generation because they can update many tokens in parallel, yet many are optimized for sequence synthesis rather than edit prediction. This setting is poorly matched to modern AI-assisted IDEs, where edit prediction must infer the next code change from recent edits, the current file, and cursor-local context. Such changes are usually sparse and preserve most source tokens, so regenerating a full code segment wastes computation. We propose Diff Diffusion, a diffusion-inspired LLM framework for code editing that predicts edit paths from an original snippet to its revised form. Diff Diffusion represents denoising as structured edit operations, and combines this formulation with multi-stage training and efficient parallel decoding. By focusing computation on changed regions, Diff Diffusion supports accurate low-latency edits and multi-position parallel modification. Across public edit-completion benchmarks, edit-prediction evaluations, and online validation, Diff Diffusion matches or leads autoregressive baselines while delivering 2.78 times faster inference on public edit-completion benchmarks and a 39.0% P50 model-latency reduction in production. This work provides a new modeling perspective for AI applications that require high accuracy and low latency.

title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation

details.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
details.abstract: COUNT adds an n-gram embedding to a transformer without adding learned parameters. At each position, it looks up the most frequent next tokens in a table of corpus n-gram counts held in CPU RAM, and adds the model’s own output-head rows for those tokens to the token embedding. Because the table lives in host memory rather than on the GPU, it can grow to hundreds of GB, and swapping in a table counted on a new domain (math, biomedical, law) adapts a trained model with no further training. With a 1B backbone COUNT matches a standard transformer trained with 57% more compute. We release the n-gram tables (17 GB to 797 GB, plus the three domain tables), and the checkpoints for COUNT and both baselines at 7 sizes from 60M to 1B parameters: https://huggingface.co/collections/IanMagnusson/count

title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision

details.title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
details.abstract: We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for testing the robustness of JEV-style decision models across text and vision, including classification, routing, tool selection, and robotics scenarios. Our public release contains 1,058 curated attack examples across five suites: meaning-preserving text attacks, text prompt injection, image perturbations, in-image instruction overlays, and instruction injection alongside images. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text and 17 on vision. One finding we found particularly interesting: resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. We also find that checking whether attacks preserve the correct answer substantially changes measured attack success. These are curated challenge sets, so the results should not be interpreted as real-world failure rates. 📊 Interactive leaderboard & examples ( https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/ ) 🤗 Dataset ( https://huggingface.co/datasets/yflantmy/DecisionRobust ) If you use decision models in an application, which failure mode would you most want a robustness benchmark to capture? We’d love suggestions for additional models and scenarios!

title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards

details.title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
details.abstract: 🚀 Can we train LLMs to collaborate, rather than only design better multi-agent workflows? I'm sharing our new preprint, Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards (CoSIR). Most LLM post-training focuses on chatbots and individual agents: instruction following, reasoning, and task completion. In multi-agent systems (MAS), however, connecting several LLMs through prompts or workflows does not guarantee effective teamwork. Agents need to learn when to share useful evidence, when to ask teammates for missing information, and how to incorporate their contributions into decisions. So we ask: can collaboration itself be an explicit target of LLM post-training? 💡 The challenge is reward design. In natural-language tasks, final success tells us little about which messages helped. A statement's value depends on what teammates already know and whether it helps them identify the correct answer. We introduce CoSIR with three components: 🔹 Scalable, verifiable environment. Agents see different parts of a rating table and must exchange information to select the best option. We can generate many tasks while tracking each agent's information and the correct answer. 🔹 Verifiable information rewards. A Bayesian evaluator scores shared evidence by its reduction in team surprisal. Requests are scored by the potential value of truthful answers, with additional rewards for correctly using received information. 🔹 Self-play RL. These fine-grained rewards directly post-train the underlying LLM, rather than only modifying an inference-time workflow. 📊 The key test is transfer to more complex tasks—not performance on the toy task alone. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it, then evaluate them on 7 unseen natural-language collaboration benchmarks spanning distributed evidence, mathematical reasoning, and collaborative decision-making. CoSIR achieves the highest seven-task score sum among compared methods on all 3 backbones (Qwen3-8B: +31.85 points versus base). We also examine behavior. For Qwen3-8B on HiddenBench, private-fact disclosure rises from 68.5% to 74.3%. In MAST-based analysis pooled across the three models, failures to use teammates' input fall from 26.3% to 22.8%, and failures to seek clarification from 36.4% to 32.0%. Performance on GSM8K, MMLU, and IFEval remains largely preserved. 🎯 Our takeaway: Collaboration is a capability that should be explicitly trained. Better workflows matter—but so does teaching the underlying LLM how to work with other agents. 📄 https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17893

title: G^3VLA: Geometric Inductive Bias for Vision-Language-Action Models

details.title: G^3VLA: Geometric Inductive Bias for Vision-Language-Action Models
details.abstract: We introduce G³VLA, a camera-aware module that helps pretrained VLAs use the geometric relationships between multiple camera views. It combines intrinsic-conditioned ray embeddings, projective positional encoding, and bidirectional cross-view fusion while preserving the policy’s action space and native imitation objective. Geometry supervision can come from ground-truth point maps or an offline π³X teacher; inference requires no depth sensor or geometry teacher. The results highlight both the value of calibrated geometry and its dependence on supervision quality and the pathway connecting visual tokens to actions. We welcome discussion on integrating geometric priors into generalist robot policies!

title: Continuum Attention

details.title: Continuum Attention
details.abstract: We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal Transformer attention operator that replaces discrete key and value lookup with integration over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve.
